stemMd:
**Council member:** Our public libraries lend books free of charge, and no one regards this as an unfair blow to the bookshops. The municipal tool library now before us would lend drills and ladders free of charge. It should likewise be regarded as no unfair blow to the shops that rent such tools out.

Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the analogy on which the council member's argument depends?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Nearly everyone who would borrow a drill or ladder from the tool library would otherwise rent one, whereas few who borrow library books would otherwise buy them.

options.label: B
options.textMd: The city's public libraries also lend musical instruments and baking equipment, and the shops that sell those goods have raised no objection.

options.label: C
options.textMd: The proposed tool library would stock only hand tools and small power tools, whereas the rental shops earn most of their revenue from heavy equipment.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Several of the city's tool-rental shops say they expect the tool library to send them customers once those customers take on larger jobs.

options.label: E
options.textMd: The tool library would be paid for out of the same municipal tax revenue, and run by the same staff, as the city's public libraries.

explanationMd:
To undermine an argument from analogy you do not attack either case on its own. You point to a difference between the two cases that matters **to the very property being transferred** from one to the other.

So begin by naming that property. The council member transfers *harmlessness to the trade*: because free lending of books does not unfairly injure bookshops, free lending of tools will not unfairly injure tool-rental shops. The unstated bridge is that the two kinds of free lending stand in the same relation to the shops' business.

That bridge is exactly what the choice about borrowers' counterfactual behaviour cuts. It reports that nearly everyone who would borrow a drill or ladder would otherwise rent one, while few who borrow library books would otherwise buy them. A book borrowed from a library is mostly a sale that was never going to happen; the shop loses a customer it did not have. A drill borrowed from the tool library is, on those figures, almost always a rental that *was* going to happen; the shop loses a customer it did have. So the harmlessness of the book case rests on a feature the tool case lacks, and the transfer fails. The two practices look alike — free lending of durable goods — and differ in the one respect the argument needs them to share.

Now test the other four by asking, of each, "which way does this push?"

- The choice about instruments and baking equipment, and the choice reporting that rental shops themselves expect new customers, both push the council member's way: the first reports a further case in which free municipal lending drew no objection, and the second has the affected businesses themselves predicting a benefit.
- The choice about the tool library stocking only hand tools and small power tools also pushes the council member's way: if the library stocks only what the shops do not chiefly live on, the injury is smaller still.
- The choice about shared tax funding and shared staff pushes neither way. Both are respects in which the two cases are *alike*, so neither can be the disanalogy the question asks for; a subsidy or a staffing arrangement that is present in the concededly harmless case cannot be what makes the new case harmful.

How to check your answer: state the disanalogy in a single sentence of the form "In the book case X, but in the tool case not-X." Only the choice about borrowers' counterfactual behaviour yields such a sentence — in the book case the borrower was not going to buy, in the tool case the borrower was going to rent — and that sentence is precisely a denial of the parallel the argument needs. If a choice cannot be phrased that way, it is not undermining an analogy, whatever else it may be doing.

distractorRationale.b: This is offered as a further parallel rather than as a disanalogy, so it pushes in the wrong direction: instruments and baking equipment are two more durable goods lent free by the city without complaint from the trade. A reader picks this by noticing that it mentions shops and lending, without checking whether it makes the two cases less alike or more.
distractorRationale.c: This reduces the predicted injury instead of exposing a difference the argument cannot survive. If the library lends only the small tools the shops do not chiefly live on, then free lending threatens the shops' revenue even less, which supports the council member's conclusion rather than undermining his reasoning.
distractorRationale.e: Shared funding and shared staff are respects in which the two cases resemble each other, not ones in which they differ, so neither can be the disanalogy the question asks for. Whatever one thinks of subsidised competition in general, a feature that is equally present in the case everyone concedes to be harmless cannot be what makes the new case harmful.
distractorRationale.d: This is testimony from the very businesses said to be threatened, and it says they expect to gain. Far from undermining the analogy, it removes the injury the objection assumes; it is chosen by readers who register that the answer should concern the rental shops without asking whether it helps or hurts the argument.

accessibilityText: A short argument by a city council member, followed by a question and five answer choices labelled A through E. The council member says that public libraries lend books free of charge without anyone regarding this as an unfair blow to bookshops, that a proposed municipal tool library would lend drills and ladders free of charge, and that it too should be regarded as no unfair blow to the shops that rent tools. The question asks which choice, if true, most seriously undermines the analogy the argument depends on. No figures, tables or mathematical notation appear.

review.author: lsat-wave4-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The analogy holds only if free lending harms rental shops no more than free book lending harms bookshops. The choice saying nearly every tool borrower would otherwise rent, while few book borrowers would otherwise buy, shows the tool library substitutes directly for shop revenue, breaking the analogy. The heavy-equipment point and the referral expectation both reduce the harm (strengthen); other lent items without objection and shared funding/staff support the similarity. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-cue-batch2-run1) reached the same answer: The analogy holds only if free lending takes business from shops to a similar degree in both cases. If almost every tool borrower would otherwise have rented, while few book borrowers would otherwise have bought, the tool library displaces far more trade, which breaks the analogy. The instruments choice and the 'send them customers' choice support the council member. The choice limiting stock to small tools suggests little harm, which also helps the conclusion. Shared funding and staff is a similarity, not a disanalogy.]

review.notes: Uniqueness was tested by attempting a defence of each choice as an undermining fact. The choices about instruments and baking equipment, about the tool library stocking only small tools, and about rental shops expecting new customers can each be defended only as strengthening the conclusion, so no reading makes them undermine the reasoning. The choice about shared tax funding was the closest call: a reader might argue that tax subsidy is itself the unfairness. It was written so that the subsidy is explicitly the same subsidy the book libraries receive, which makes it a shared feature and therefore unavailable as a disanalogy — a point spelled out in its rationale. Only the choice about what borrowers would otherwise have done states a difference in the property the analogy transfers. Awaiting blind independent solve; author must not publish this item.
